claim: Sulfakinin (SK)/cholecystokinin (CCK)-type neuropeptides regulate feeding and digestion in protostomes (e.g. insects) and chordates.
source: Sulfakinin (SK)/cholecystokinin (CCK)-type neuropeptides regulate feeding and digestion in protostomes (e.g. insects) and chordates.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work on SK/CCK-type signaling in various taxa.

claim: Two neuropeptides (ArSK/CCK1, ArSK/CCK2) derived from the precursor protein ArSK/CCKP act as ligands for an SK/CCK-type receptor (ArSK/CCKR) in Asterias rubens.
source: In this species, two neuropeptides (ArSK/CCK1, ArSK/CCK2) derived from the precursor protein ArSK/CCKP act as ligands for an SK/CCK-type receptor (ArSK/CCKR)
evidence: Supported by receptor activation assays shown in Figure 3 and mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 peptides/proteins are expressed in the nervous system, digestive system, tube feet, and body wall of Asterias rubens.
source: these peptides/proteins are expressed in the nervous system, digestive system, tube feet, and body wall.
evidence: Supported by mRNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4 and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 cause dose-dependent contraction of cardiac stomach preparations in vitro.
source: ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 cause dose-dependent contraction of cardiac stomach, tube foot, and apical muscle preparations in vitro
evidence: Supported by in vitro pharmacology data shown in Figure 7a and 7b.

claim: ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 cause dose-dependent contraction of tube foot preparations in vitro.
source: ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 cause dose-dependent contraction of cardiac stomach, tube foot, and apical muscle preparations in vitro
evidence: Supported by in vitro pharmacology data shown in Figure 7c and 7d.

claim: ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 cause dose-dependent contraction of apical muscle preparations in vitro.
source: ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 cause dose-dependent contraction of cardiac stomach, tube foot, and apical muscle preparations in vitro
evidence: Supported by in vitro pharmacology data shown in Figure 7e and 7f.

claim: Injection of ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 in vivo triggers cardiac stomach retraction in A. rubens.
source: injection of these neuropeptides in vivo triggers cardiac stomach retraction
evidence: Supported by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Injection of ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK2 in vivo inhibits the onset of feeding in A. rubens.
source: injection of these neuropeptides in vivo triggers cardiac stomach retraction and inhibition of the onset of feeding in A. rubens.
evidence: Supported by feeding behavior experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: An evolutionarily ancient role of SK/CCK-type neuropeptides as inhibitory regulators of feeding-related processes in the Bilateria has been conserved in echinoderms.
source: Thus, an evolutionarily ancient role of SK/CCK-type neuropeptides as inhibitory regulators of feeding-related processes in the Bilateria has been conserved in the unusual and unique context of the extra-oral feeding behaviour and pentaradial body plan of an echinoderm.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data from this study combined with comparative knowledge from other taxa.

claim: Cholecystokinin (CCK) was discovered and named on account of its effects as a stimulator of gall bladder contraction in mammals.
source: The peptide hormones cholecystokinin (CCK) and gastrin were discovered and named on account of their effects as stimulators of gall bladder contraction and gastric secretion of pepsin/acid, respectively, in mammals (Edkins, 1906; Ivy ACO and Goldberg, 1928).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical literature (Ivy ACO and Goldberg, 1928).

claim: Gastrin was discovered and named on account of its effects as a stimulator of gastric secretion of pepsin/acid in mammals.
source: The peptide hormones cholecystokinin (CCK) and gastrin were discovered and named on account of their effects as stimulators of gall bladder contraction and gastric secretion of pepsin/acid, respectively, in mammals (Edkins, 1906; Ivy ACO and Goldberg, 1928).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical literature (Edkins, 1906).

claim: CCK and gastrin have the same C-terminal structural motif (Trp-Met-Asp-Phe-NH2).
source: Determination of the structures of CCK and gastrin revealed that they have the same C-terminal structural motif (Trp-Met-Asp-Phe-NH2), indicative of a common evolutionary origin (Gregory et al., 1964; Mutt and Jorpes, 1968).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies (Gregory et al., 1964; Mutt and Jorpes, 1968).

claim: CCK and gastrin are derived from different precursor proteins.
source: However, CCK and gastrin are derived from different precursor proteins, which are subject to cell/tissue-specific processing to give rise to bioactive peptides of varying length (e.g. CCK-8 and CCK-33; gastrin-17 and gastrin-34) (Boel et al., 1983; Deschenes et al., 1984; Rehfeld et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to molecular studies (Boel et al., 1983; Deschenes et al., 1984; Rehfeld et al., 2007).

claim: CCK and gastrin have a tyrosine residue that can be sulphated post-translationally.
source: Furthermore, CCK and gastrin have a tyrosine residue at positions 7 and 6 from the C-terminal amide, respectively, which can be sulphated post-translationally (Rehfeld et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to review (Rehfeld et al., 2007).

claim: The effects of CCK and gastrin in mammals are mediated by two G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), CCK-A (CCKR1) and CCK-B (CCKR2).
source: The effects of CCK and gastrin in mammals are mediated by two G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), CCK-A (CCKR1) and CCK-B (CCKR2), with both sulphated and non-sulphated forms of CCK and gastrin acting as ligands for the CCK-B receptor, whilst the CCK-A receptor is selectively activated by sulphated CCK (de Weerth et al., 1993; Dufresne et al., 2006; Kopin et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1993; Noble and Roques, 1999; Wank et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to receptor characterization studies.

claim: The CCK-A receptor is selectively activated by sulphated CCK.
source: The effects of CCK and gastrin in mammals are mediated by two G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), CCK-A (CCKR1) and CCK-B (CCKR2), with both sulphated and non-sulphated forms of CCK and gastrin acting as ligands for the CCK-B receptor, whilst the CCK-A receptor is selectively activated by sulphated CCK (de Weerth et al., 1993; Dufresne et al., 2006; Kopin et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1993; Noble and Roques, 1999; Wank et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to receptor pharmacology studies.

claim: Both sulphated and non-sulphated forms of CCK and gastrin act as ligands for the CCK-B receptor.
source: The effects of CCK and gastrin in mammals are mediated by two G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), CCK-A (CCKR1) and CCK-B (CCKR2), with both sulphated and non-sulphated forms of CCK and gastrin acting as ligands for the CCK-B receptor, whilst the CCK-A receptor is selectively activated by sulphated CCK (de Weerth et al., 1993; Dufresne et al., 2006; Kopin et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1993; Noble and Roques, 1999; Wank et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to receptor pharmacology studies.

claim: Gastrin stimulates growth of the stomach lining in mammals.
source: Thus, in the gastrointestinal system, gastrin stimulates growth of the stomach lining, gastric contractions, and gastric emptying (Crean et al., 1969; Dockray et al., 2005; Gregory and Tracy, 1964; Vizi et al., 1973)
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies (Crean et al., 1969; Dockray et al., 2005; Gregory and Tracy, 1964; Vizi et al., 1973).

claim: Gastrin stimulates gastric contractions in mammals.
source: Thus, in the gastrointestinal system, gastrin stimulates growth of the stomach lining, gastric contractions, and gastric emptying (Crean et al., 1969; Dockray et al., 2005; Gregory and Tracy, 1964; Vizi et al., 1973)
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Gastrin stimulates gastric emptying in mammals.
source: Thus, in the gastrointestinal system, gastrin stimulates growth of the stomach lining, gastric contractions, and gastric emptying (Crean et al., 1969; Dockray et al., 2005; Gregory and Tracy, 1964; Vizi et al., 1973)
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion in mammals.
source: whilst CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, contraction of the pyloric sphincter, and intestinal motility (Chen et al., 2004; Gutiérrez et al., 1974; Harper and Raper, 1943; Rehfeld, 2017; Shaw and Jones, 1978; Vizi et al., 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: CCK stimulates contraction of the pyloric sphincter in mammals.
source: whilst CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, contraction of the pyloric sphincter, and intestinal motility (Chen et al., 2004; Gutiérrez et al., 1974; Harper and Raper, 1943; Rehfeld, 2017; Shaw and Jones, 1978; Vizi et al., 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: CCK stimulates intestinal motility in mammals.
source: whilst CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, contraction of the pyloric sphincter, and intestinal motility (Chen et al., 2004; Gutiérrez et al., 1974; Harper and Raper, 1943; Rehfeld, 2017; Shaw and Jones, 1978; Vizi et al., 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: CCK inhibits food intake as a mediator of satiety in mammals.
source: Furthermore, CCK also has behavioural effects that include inhibition of food intake as a mediator of satiety and stimulation of aggression and anxiogenesis (Chandra and Liddle, 2007; Gibbs et al., 1973; Singh et al., 1991; Smith et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies (Chandra and Liddle, 2007; Gibbs et al., 1973; Smith et al., 1981).

claim: CCK stimulates aggression in mammals.
source: Furthermore, CCK also has behavioural effects that include inhibition of food intake as a mediator of satiety and stimulation of aggression and anxiogenesis (Chandra and Liddle, 2007; Gibbs et al., 1973; Singh et al., 1991; Smith et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies (Singh et al., 1991).

claim: CCK stimulates anxiogenesis in mammals.
source: Furthermore, CCK also has behavioural effects that include inhibition of food intake as a mediator of satiety and stimulation of aggression and anxiogenesis (Chandra and Liddle, 2007; Gibbs et al., 1973; Singh et al., 1991; Smith et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Genome duplication in a common ancestor of the vertebrates gave rise to genes encoding CCK-type and gastrin-type precursor proteins.
source: Phylogenomic studies indicate that genome duplication in a common ancestor of the vertebrates gave rise to genes encoding CCK-type and gastrin-type precursor proteins (Dupré and Tostivint, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to phylogenomic study (Dupré and Tostivint, 2014).

claim: Invertebrate chordates have a single gene encoding a 'hybrid' CCK/gastrin-like peptide.
source: Accordingly, invertebrate chordates that are the closest extant relatives of vertebrates (e.g. the urochordate Ciona intestinalis) have a single gene encoding a 'hybrid' CCK/gastrin-like peptide (e.g. cionin) with a sulphated tyrosine residue at both positions 6 and 7 from the C-terminal amide (Johnsen and Rehfeld, 1990; Monstein et al., 1993; Thorndyke and Dockray, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on urochordates (Johnsen and Rehfeld, 1990; Monstein et al., 1993; Thorndyke and Dockray, 1986).

claim: CCK-type peptides stimulate gastric enzyme secretion in the sea squirt Styela clava.
source: Furthermore, CCK-type peptides stimulate gastric enzyme secretion in the sea squirt Styela clava, providing evidence of evolutionarily ancient roles as regulators of gastrointestinal physiology in chordates (Bevis and Thorndyke, 1981; Thorndyke and Bevis, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on sea squirts (Bevis and Thorndyke, 1981; Thorndyke and Bevis, 1984).

claim: Substances immunoreactive with antibodies to CCK and/or gastrin have been detected in a variety of invertebrates, including arthropods, annelids, molluscs, and cnidarians.
source: Evidence that the phylogenetic distribution of CCK/gastrin-type peptides may extend beyond chordates to other phyla was first obtained with the detection of substances immunoreactive with antibodies to CCK and/or gastrin in a variety of invertebrates, including arthropods, annelids, molluscs, and cnidarians (Dockray et al., 1981; El-Salhy et al., 1980; Grimmelikhuijzen et al., 1980; Kramer et al., 1977; Larson and Vigna, 1983; Rzasa et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to immunohistochemical studies (Dockray et al., 1981; El-Salhy et al., 1980; Grimmelikhuijzen et al., 1980; Kramer et al., 1977; Larson and Vigna, 1983; Rzasa et al., 1982).

claim: Leucosulfakinin is a CCK-like peptide isolated from the insect Leucophaea maderae.
source: However, molecular evidence of the evolutionary antiquity of CCK/gastrin-type signalling was obtained with the purification and sequencing of a CCK-like peptide named leucosulfakinin, which was isolated from the insect (cockroach) Leucophaea maderae (Nachman et al., 1986a).
evidence: Supported by citation to peptide isolation study (Nachman et al., 1986a).

claim: GPCRs that are homologs of the vertebrate CCKA/CCKB-type receptors have been identified and pharmacologically characterised as receptors for sulfakinin (SK)-type peptides in a variety of insects, including Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Subsequently, GPCRs that are homologs of the vertebrate CCKA/CCKB-type receptors have been identified and pharmacologically characterised as receptors for sulfakinin (SK)-type peptides in a variety of insects, including Drosophila melanogaster (Bloom et al., 2019; Kubiak et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2013b; Yu and Smagghe, 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to receptor characterization studies (Bloom et al., 2019; Kubiak et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2013b; Yu and Smagghe, 2014b).

claim: SK-type peptides have myotropic effects on the gut in several insect species.
source: Thus, in several insect species SK-type peptides have myotropic effects on the gut (Al-Alkawi et al., 2017; Marciniak et al., 2011; Nachman et al., 1986a; Nachman et al., 1986b; Nichols, 2007; Palmer et al., 2007; Predel et al., 2001; Schoofs et al., 1990)
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies on insects.

claim: SK-type peptides affect digestive enzyme release in insects.
source: and/or affect digestive enzyme release (Harshini et al., 2002a; Harshini et al., 2002b; Nachman et al., 1997; Zels et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies on insects (Harshini et al., 2002a; Harshini et al., 2002b; Nachman et al., 1997; Zels et al., 2015).

claim: SK-type peptides act as satiety factors in insects.
source: Furthermore, at a behavioural level there is evidence that SK-type peptides act as satiety factors (Al-Alkawi et al., 2017; Bloom et al., 2019; Downer et al., 2007; Maestro et al., 2001; Meyering-Vos and Müller, 2007; Nässel and Zandawala, 2019; Nichols et al., 2008; Wei, 2000; Yu et al., 2013a; Yu et al., 2013b; Yu and Smagghe, 2014b; Zels et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies on insects.

claim: SK-type peptides regulate locomotion in insects.
source: and regulate locomotion and aggression in insects (Chen et al., 2012; Nässel and Williams, 2014; Nässel and Zandawala, 2019; Nichols et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies on insects (Chen et al., 2012; Nässel and Williams, 2014; Nässel and Zandawala, 2019; Nichols et al., 2008).

claim: SK-type peptides regulate aggression in insects.
source: and regulate locomotion and aggression in insects (Chen et al., 2012; Nässel and Williams, 2014; Nässel and Zandawala, 2019; Nichols et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies on insects.

claim: The evolutionary origin of SK/CCK-type signalling can be traced back to the common ancestor of the Bilateria.
source: The discovery and functional characterisation of SK-type signalling in insects and other arthropods indicated that the evolutionary origin SK/CCK-type signalling can be traced back to the common ancestor of the Bilateria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of SK/CCK-type signaling systems.

claim: SK/CCK-type signalling systems have been discovered in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, the mollusc Crassostrea gigas, and the annelid Capitella teleta.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, SK/CCK-type signalling systems have been discovered in a variety of protostome invertebrates, including the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, the mollusc Crassostrea gigas, and the annelid Capitella teleta (Janssen et al., 2008; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Schwartz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on these species (Janssen et al., 2008; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Schwartz et al., 2018).

claim: SK/CCK-type peptides cause a decrease in the frequency of spontaneous contractions of the Crassostrea gigas hindgut.
source: Furthermore, some insights into the physiological roles of SK/CCK-type signalling in non-arthropod protostomes have been obtained, including causing a decrease in the frequency of spontaneous contractions of the C. gigas hindgut (Schwartz et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to study on C. gigas (Schwartz et al., 2018).

claim: SK/CCK-type peptides stimulate digestive enzyme secretion in Caenorhabditis elegans and Pecten maximus.
source: stimulation of digestive enzyme secretion in C. elegans and Pecten maximus (Nachman et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to study (Nachman et al., 1997).

claim: SK/CCK-type peptides have a role in regulation of feeding and energy storage in Crassostrea gigas.
source: and evidence of a role in regulation of feeding and energy storage in C. gigas (Schwartz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on C. gigas (Schwartz et al., 2018).

claim: CCK-like immunoreactive cells have been revealed in the intestine of sea cucumbers.
source: Prior to the genome sequencing era, use of immunohistochemical methods revealed CCK-like immunoreactive cells in the intestine of sea cucumbers (phylum Echinodermata) and vertebrate CCK/gastrin-type peptides were found to cause relaxation of sea cucumber intestine (García-Arrarás et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to immunohistochemical study (García-Arrarás et al., 1991).

claim: Vertebrate CCK/gastrin-type peptides cause relaxation of sea cucumber intestine.
source: Prior to the genome sequencing era, use of immunohistochemical methods revealed CCK-like immunoreactive cells in the intestine of sea cucumbers (phylum Echinodermata) and vertebrate CCK/gastrin-type peptides were found to cause relaxation of sea cucumber intestine (García-Arrarás et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to pharmacological study (García-Arrarás et al., 1991).

claim: Transcripts/genes encoding SK/CCK-type peptide precursors and SK/CCK-type receptors have been identified in echinoderms and hemichordates.
source: More recently, analysis of transcriptome/genome sequence data has enabled identification of transcripts/genes encoding SK/CCK-type peptide precursors and SK/CCK-type receptors in echinoderms and hemichordates (Burke et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2019; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Semmens et al., 2016; Zandawala et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to genomic/transcriptomic studies (Burke et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2019; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Semmens et al., 2016; Zandawala et al., 2017).

claim: Functional characterisation of native SK/CCK-type peptides and receptors has not been reported for an echinoderm or hemichordate species prior to this study.
source: However, functional characterisation of native SK/CCK-type peptides and receptors has yet to be reported for an echinoderm or hemichordate species.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: Asterias rubens has been established as an experimental model for molecular and functional characterisation of neuropeptides.
source: We have established the common European starfish Asterias rubens as an experimental model for molecular and functional characterisation of neuropeptides, obtaining novel insights into the evolution and comparative physiology of several neuropeptide signalling systems (Cai et al., 2018; Elphick et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2017a; Lin et al., 2018; Odekunle et al., 2019; Semmens and Elphick, 2017; Tian et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2016; Tinoco et al., 2018; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2018; Yañez-Guerra et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors' group.

claim: The cloned cDNA sequence encoding ArSK/CCKP confirmed the sequence obtained from transcriptome data.
source: Here, cloning and sequencing of a cDNA encoding ArSK/CCKP confirmed the sequence obtained from transcriptome data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by the cDNA sequence shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ArSK/CCKP comprises two putative SK/CCK-type neuropeptide sequences that are bounded by dibasic or tetrabasic cleavage sites.
source: ArSK/CCKP comprises two putative SK/CCK-type neuropeptide sequences that are bounded by dibasic or tetrabasic cleavage sites.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Both neuropeptide sequences in ArSK/CCKP have a C-terminal glycine residue, which is a potential substrate for post-translational amidation.
source: Both neuropeptide sequences have a C-terminal glycine residue, which is a potential substrate for post-translational amidation
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and knowledge of post-translational modifications.

claim: Both neuropeptide sequences in ArSK/CCKP contain a tyrosine residue, which could be either sulphated or non-sulphated in the mature neuropeptides.
source: and both neuropeptide sequences contain a tyrosine residue, which could be either sulphated or non-sulphated (ns) in the mature neuropeptides.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and knowledge of post-translational modifications.

claim: An N-terminal glutamine residue (Q) in one of the neuropeptide sequences in ArSK/CCKP is a potential substrate for N-terminal pyroglutamylation (pQ).
source: Furthermore, an N-terminal glutamine residue (Q) in one of the neuropeptide sequences is a potential substrate for N-terminal pyroglutamylation (pQ) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and knowledge of post-translational modifications.

claim: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of pQSKVDDY(SO3H)GHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1).
source: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of four SK/CCK-type peptides derived from ArSK/CCKP: pQSKVDDY(SO3H)GHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of pQSKVDDYGHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1(ns)).
source: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of four SK/CCK-type peptides derived from ArSK/CCKP: pQSKVDDY(SO3H)GHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), pQSKVDDYGHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1(ns); Figure 1—figure supplement 2c)
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of GGDDQY(SO3H)GFGLFF-NH2 (ArSK/CCK2).
source: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of four SK/CCK-type peptides derived from ArSK/CCKP: pQSKVDDY(SO3H)GHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), pQSKVDDYGHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1(ns); Figure 1—figure supplement 2c), GGDDQY(SO3H)GFGLFF-NH2 (ArSK/CCK2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2d)
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d.

claim: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of GGDDQYGFGLFF-NH2 (ArSK/CCK2(ns)).
source: LC-MS-MS analysis of A. rubens radial nerve cord extracts revealed the presence of four SK/CCK-type peptides derived from ArSK/CCKP: pQSKVDDY(SO3H)GHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), pQSKVDDYGHGLFW-NH2 (ArSK/CCK1(ns); Figure 1—figure supplement 2c), GGDDQY(SO3H)GFGLFF-NH2 (ArSK/CCK2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2d), and GGDDQYGFGLFF-NH2 (ArSK/CCK2(ns); Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e.

claim: Mass spectrometry confirmed that the ArSK/CCKP-derived peptides are C-terminally amidated.
source: Thus, mass spectrometry confirmed that (i) the peptides are C-terminally amidated
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mass spectrometry confirmed that the ArSK/CCKP-derived peptides are detected with or without tyrosine sulphation.
source: Thus, mass spectrometry confirmed that (i) the peptides are C-terminally amidated, (ii) the peptides are detected with or without tyrosine sulphation
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mass spectrometry confirmed that an N-terminal glutamine is post-translationally converted to pyroglutamate in the mature ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK1(ns) peptides.
source: Thus, mass spectrometry confirmed that (i) the peptides are C-terminally amidated, (ii) the peptides are detected with or without tyrosine sulphation, and (iii) an N-terminal glutamine is post-translationally converted to pyroglutamate in the mature ArSK/CCK1 and ArSK/CCK1(ns) peptides.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SK/CCK-type peptides have several evolutionarily conserved features, including a tyrosine residue (typically sulphated) and a C-terminal amide group that are separated by five to seven intervening residues.
source: This revealed several evolutionarily conserved features, including a tyrosine residue (typically sulphated) and a C-terminal amide group that are separated by five to seven intervening residues.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1.

claim: The C-terminal residue in most SK/CCK-type peptides, including ArSK/CCK2, is a phenylalanine residue.
source: The C-terminal residue in most SK/CCK-type peptides, including ArSK/CCK2, is a phenylalanine residue.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1.

claim: ArSK/CCK1 is atypical in having a C-terminal tryptophan residue.
source: However, ArSK/CCK1 is atypical in having a C-terminal tryptophan residue, which is also a feature of an SK/CCK-type peptide in the bivalve mollusc C. gigas.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1.

claim: An SK/CCK-type peptide in the bivalve mollusc C. gigas has a C-terminal tryptophan residue.
source: However, ArSK/CCK1 is atypical in having a C-terminal tryptophan residue, which is also a feature of an SK/CCK-type peptide in the bivalve mollusc C. gigas.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1.

claim: ArSK/CCKR is an ortholog of SK/CCK-type receptors that have been characterised in other taxa.
source: Thus, this demonstrates that ArSK/CCKR is an ortholog of SK/CCK-type receptors that have been characterised in other taxa.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: ArSK/CCKR is positioned within a branch of the phylogenetic tree that comprises SK/CCK-type receptors from deuterostomes.
source: Furthermore, reflecting known animal phylogenetic relationships, ArSK/CCKR is positioned within a branch of the tree that comprises SK/CCK-type receptors from deuterostomes
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: ArSK/CCKR is positioned within an ambulacrarian clade that comprises SK/CCK-type receptors from other echinoderms and from the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
source: and more specifically it is positioned within an ambulacrarian clade that comprises SK/CCK-type receptors from other echinoderms and from the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: ArSK/CCKR has seven predicted transmembrane domains.
source: Analysis of the amino acid sequence of ArSK/CCKR using the Protter tool (Omasits et al., 2014) revealed seven predicted transmembrane domains, as expected for a GPCR
evidence: Supported by topology prediction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: ArSK/CCKR has three potential N-glycosylation sites in the predicted extracellular N-terminal region.
source: and three potential N-glycosylation sites in the predicted extracellular N-terminal region of the receptor (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by topology prediction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: ArSK/CCK1 caused concentration-dependent stimulation of luminescence in CHO-K1 cells transfected with ArSK/CCKR with an EC50 value of 0.25 nM.
source: However, all three peptides caused concentration-dependent stimulation of luminescence in CHO-K1 cells transfected with ArSK/CCKR (Figure 3). The EC50 values for ArSK/CCK1, ArSK/CCK2, and ArSK/CCK2(ns) were 0.25 nM (Figure 3a)
evidence: Supported by receptor activation assay data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: ArSK/CCK2 caused concentration-dependent stimulation of luminescence in CHO-K1 cells transfected with ArSK/CCKR with an EC50 value of 0.12 nM.

evidence: Supported by comparison with literature on SK/CCK-type signaling in other taxa (Dufresne et al., 2006; Kubiak et al., 2002).

claim: Non-sulphated SK/CCK-type peptides act as potent ligands for CCK2R in mammals.
source: However, this is not a universal feature of SK/CCK-type signalling; for example, non-sulphated SK/CCK-type peptides act as potent ligands for CCK2R in mammals (Dufresne et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to review (Dufresne et al., 2006).

claim: In ArSK/CCK1, ArSK/CCK2, and SK/CCK-type peptides from other echinoderms and hemichordates (collectively Ambulacraria), there are six intervening residues between the tyrosine and the C-terminal amide.
source: Accordingly, in ArSK/CCK1, ArSK/CCK2, and SK/CCK-type peptides from other echinoderms and hemichordates (collectively Ambulacraria), there are six intervening residues.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1.

claim: A DYG motif is a feature of many SK/CCK-type peptides in lophotrochozoans and arthropods.
source: In ArSK/CCK1 the tyrosine (Y) residue is preceded by an aspartate (D) residue and the tyrosine (Y) residue is followed by a glycine (G) residue; accordingly, a DYG motif is also a feature of many SK/CCK-type peptides in lophotrochozoans and arthropods
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1.

claim: The DYG motif may be an ancestral characteristic of SK/CCK-type peptides that has been lost in some bilaterian taxa (e.g. chordates, nematodes).
source: suggesting that this may be an ancestral characteristic that has been lost in some bilaterian taxa (e.g. chordates, nematodes).

claim: N-terminal pyroglutamate is predicted or known to occur in some SK/CCK-type peptides in other taxa, including the SK1 and SK2 peptides from the cockroach L. maderae and the SK/CCK-type peptides in the molluscs Pinctata fucata and C. gigas.
source: ArSK/CCK1, but not ArSK/CCK2, has an N-terminal pyroglutamate in its mature form and this post-translational modification is also predicted or known to occur in some SK/CCK-type peptides in other taxa – for example, the SK1 and SK2 peptides from the cockroach L. maderae (Predel et al., 1999) and the SK/CCK-type peptides in the molluscs Pinctata fucata and C. gigas (Schwartz et al., 2018; Stewart et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on other species (Predel et al., 1999; Schwartz et al., 2018; Stewart et al., 2014).

claim: SK/CCK-type peptides with a C-terminal tryptophan (W) residue evolved independently in starfish and in the bivalve mollusc C. gigas.

evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of this feature.

claim: SK/CCK-type neuropeptides released by the axonal processes of mucosal neurons located in the basiepithelial nerve plexus may cause stomach contraction by acting directly on visceral muscle and/or indirectly by triggering the release of other myoactive substances from the basiepithelial nerve plexus.

evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data from this study combined with comparative knowledge from other taxa.

claim: Findings from starfish reveal how ancient roles of neuropeptide signalling systems have been preserved in spite of unique and radical evolutionary and developmental changes in the anatomy of echinoderms amongst bilaterian animals.
source: Thus, our findings from starfish reported here for SK/CCK-type neuropeptides and previously for other neuropeptides (Cai et al., 2018; Odekunle et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2017; Tinoco et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020) reveal how ancient roles of neuropeptide signalling systems have been preserved in spite of unique and radical evolutionary and developmental changes in the anatomy of echinoderms amongst bilaterian animals.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data from this study and previous studies by the authors' group, combined with evolutionary considerations.
